claims.claim: Low density bone was doubled in the proximal region of 12 week old Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice compared to Dmp1Cre mice.
claims.source: This was most notable in low density bone which was doubled in the proximal region compared to Dmp1Cre mice; this was statistically significant (Figure 3—figure supplement 2 shows comparisons between genotypes at each slice and bone density level).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: In 12 week old Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, the proportion of low density bone reduced significantly with distance from the growth plate, as mid-density bone increased.
claims.source: The proportion of low density bone reduced significantly with distance from the growth plate, as mid-density bone increased (distance effect, p<0.0001 for both).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: In 12 week old Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, there was no significant change in the very low proportion of high density bone, which was absent in most samples even in the proximal slices.
claims.source: There was no significant change in the very low proportion of high density bone, which was absent in most samples even in the proximal slices.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: 12 week old Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora accumulate mid-density bone in regions furthest from the growth plate in the same manner as the control mice, but it is on the background of a high level of immature low density bone.
claims.source: Their femora accumulate mid-density bone in regions furthest from the growth plate in the same manner as the control mice, but it is on the background of a high level of immature low density bone.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the slice-by-slice analysis data.

claims.claim: At 15 weeks of age the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora had more high density bone in regions furthest from the growth plate.
claims.source: At 15 weeks of age the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora, like the Dmp1Cre femora, had more high density bone in regions furthest from the growth plate (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Although Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora started with a lower level of high density bone than controls at 15 weeks, they reached the same level of high density bone.
claims.source: Although Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora started with a lower level of high density bone than controls, they reached the same level of high density bone (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora at 15 weeks of age had more low density bone than age-matched controls in the region closest to the growth plate.
claims.source: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora at 15 weeks of age also had more low density bone than age-matched controls in the region closest to the growth plate, as at 12 weeks (Figure 3—figure supplement 2); and unlike age-matched Dmp1Cre controls, this declined significantly along the length of the bone.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: In 15 week old Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora, low density bone declined significantly along the length of the bone, unlike age-matched Dmp1Cre controls.
claims.source: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora at 15 weeks of age also had more low density bone than age-matched controls in the region closest to the growth plate, as at 12 weeks (Figure 3—figure supplement 2); and unlike age-matched Dmp1Cre controls, this declined significantly along the length of the bone.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora at 15 weeks had a higher proportion of mid-density bone compared to controls along almost the full length of the metaphysis.
claims.source: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora also had a higher proportion of mid-density bone compared to controls along almost the full length of the metaphysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora exhibit both the reduction in cortical porosity and the increase in bone density associated with corticalisation, but this process occurs in the presence of a greater quantity of low density bone than in control mice of the same age and sex.
claims.source: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora therefore exhibit both the reduction in cortical porosity and the increase in bone density associated with corticalisation. However, this process occurs in the presence of a greater quantity of low density bone than in control mice of the same age and sex.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data showing changes in cortical porosity and bone density distribution.

claims.claim: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice have immature cortical bone compared with their age-matched controls.
claims.source: This confirms that Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice have immature cortical bone compared with their age-matched controls.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data showing differences in bone density distribution and histological appearance.

claims.claim: At 16 weeks old, in approximately 40% of the bone closest to the endocortical edge, control bone exhibited mature lamellar bone, characterised by flattened and aligned osteocytes with dendritic processes primarily running perpendicular to the endocortical surface.
claims.source: At this site, in approximately 40% of the bone closest to the endocortical edge, control bone exhibited mature lamellar bone, characterised by flattened and aligned osteocytes with dendritic processes primarily running perpendicular to the endocortical surface (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Ploton silver staining shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Osteocytes in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone at 16 weeks old were more rounded, showed no ordered orientation, and the bone contained many cement lines.
claims.source: In contrast, osteocytes in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone at the same anatomical location were more rounded, showed no ordered orientation, and the bone contained many cement lines (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Ploton silver staining shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: The newly forming Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f cortical bone does not contain cartilage remnants.
claims.source: Since we have previously reported that the newly forming Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f cortical bone does not contain cartilage remnants (Cho et al., 2017), the abundant cement lines of Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f cortical bone do not reflect retention of immature endochondral cartilage and woven bone.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cho et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The abundant cement lines of Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f cortical bone reflect rapid remodelling and replacement of that structure with woven bone.
claims.source: Since we have previously reported that the newly forming Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f cortical bone does not contain cartilage remnants (Cho et al., 2017), the abundant cement lines of Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f cortical bone do not reflect retention of immature endochondral cartilage and woven bone. Rather, it reflects rapid remodelling and replacement of that structure with woven bone.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the histological observations and previous findings.

claims.claim: Although the control cortical bone had accrued lamellar bone at 16 weeks, this has not occurred in the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f cortex.
claims.source: Although the control cortical bone had accrued lamellar bone at this time point, this has not occurred in the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f cortex.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histological observations shown in Figures 3F and 3G.

claims.claim: Female Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora at 26 weeks had normal bone mass but significantly less high- and mid- density bone, and more low-density bone than controls.
claims.source: Using our three-tiered density analysis, we observed that although female Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f femora had normal bone mass, they still had significantly less high- and mid- density bone, and more low-density bone than controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice showed prolonged STAT3 phosphorylation in response to all IL-6 family cytokines tested (IL-11, LIF and OSM) compared to Dmp1Cre mice.
claims.source: When tested in a calvarial injection model, Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice showed prolonged STAT3 phosphorylation in response to all IL-6 family cytokines tested (IL-11, LIF and OSM) compared to Dmp1Cre mice (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: There was no STAT3 phosphorylation response to either Leptin or G-CSF in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
claims.source: In contrast, there was no STAT3 phosphorylation response to either Leptin or G-CSF (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on experimental data not shown in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f phenotype may result from prolonged STAT3 phosphorylation downstream of gp130 binding cytokines, including IL-11, LIF and OSM.
claims.source: The Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f phenotype may therefore result from prolonged STAT3 phosphorylation downstream of gp130 binding cytokines, including IL-11, LIF and OSM.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the STAT3 phosphorylation data.

claims.claim: There was no difference in basal phospho-STAT3 levels detected by western blot between Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f and control mice.
claims.source: There was no difference in basal phospho-STAT3 levels detected by western blot, consistent with observations in other cell-specific knockouts of SOCS3 (Croker et al., 2003; Croker et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data and citations to Croker et al., 2003 and 2004.

claims.claim: The lack of difference in basal phospho-STAT3 levels is likely due to the low level of STAT3 phosphorylation in basal conditions relative to the stimulated response, or may reflect that the tissue contains a mixture of cell types, including cells with normal levels of SOCS3.
claims.source: This is likely due to the low level of STAT3 phosphorylation in basal conditions relative to the stimulated response, or may reflect that the tissue contains a mixture of cell types, including cells with normal levels of SOCS3.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the reasons for the lack of difference in basal phospho-STAT3 levels.

claims.claim: STAT3 phosphorylation was elevated in osteocytes in both male and female tibial samples from Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
claims.source: STAT3 phosphorylation was elevated in osteocytes by immunohistochemical quantitation of phospho-STAT3 positive osteocytes, which were significantly elevated in both male and female tibial samples (Figure 4D), confirming that a lack of SOCS3 negative feedback results in elevated STAT3 signalling in response to endogenous stimuli.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: A lack of SOCS3 negative feedback results in elevated STAT3 signalling in response to endogenous stimuli.
claims.source: STAT3 phosphorylation was elevated in osteocytes by immunohistochemical quantitation of phospho-STAT3 positive osteocytes, which were significantly elevated in both male and female tibial samples (Figure 4D), confirming that a lack of SOCS3 negative feedback results in elevated STAT3 signalling in response to endogenous stimuli.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the immunohistochemistry data.

claims.claim: The Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f phenotype is not rescued by IL-6 deletion.
claims.source: We previously reported that the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f phenotype is not rescued by IL-6 deletion (Cho et al., 2017), and since all other gp130-binding cytokines tested induced prolonged phosphorylation, we next determined whether gp130 deletion in osteocytes might resolve the phenotype.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cho et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The previously published gp130-flox mouse is reported to increase release of soluble gp130 by targeted cells.
claims.source: The rationale for this was that the gp130-flox mouse we previously utilised (Standal et al., 2014; Johnson et al., 2014) is reported to increase release of soluble gp130 by targeted cells (Betz et al., 1998), which might act locally as an inhibitor of signalling in other cell types.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Standal et al., 2014, Johnson et al., 2014, and Betz et al., 1998.

claims.claim: The new mouse with Dmp1Cre targeted deletion (Dmp1Cre:Il6stf/f) showed reduced Il6st transcription in bone.
claims.source: The new mouse with Dmp1Cre targeted deletion (Dmp1Cre:Il6stf/f) showed reduced Il6st transcription in bone (Table 1) and exhibited a similar phenotype to that observed with the previously published gp130 targeting strategy (Dmp1Cre:gp130f/f).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by mRNA data shown in Table 1.

claims.claim: The Dmp1Cre:Il6stf/f mouse exhibited low trabecular bone mass, increased periosteal circumference, and reduced bone formation with no reduction in bone resorption.
claims.source: The new mouse with Dmp1Cre targeted deletion (Dmp1Cre:Il6stf/f) showed reduced Il6st transcription in bone (Table 1) and exhibited a similar phenotype to that observed with the previously published gp130 targeting strategy (Dmp1Cre:gp130f/f). That is, the mouse exhibited low trabecular bone mass, increased periosteal circumference, and reduced bone formation with no reduction in bone resorption (Table 1; Standal et al., 2014; Johnson et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Table 1 and citations to Standal et al., 2014 and Johnson et al., 2014.

claims.claim: gp130 in osteocytes is required for normal bone formation and normal trabecular bone mass.
claims.source: This confirmed our earlier finding that gp130 in osteocytes is required for normal bone formation and normal trabecular bone mass.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the Dmp1Cre:Il6stf/f phenotype and previous findings.

claims.claim: Dmp1Cre:Il6stf/f mice had normal cortical porosity.
claims.source: When Dmp1Cre:Il6stf/f mice, which themselves had normal cortical porosity (Figure 5A) were crossed with Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, the resulting Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice exhibited normalised cortical porosity at 12 weeks of age in both male and female mice (Figure 5B,C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice exhibited normalised cortical porosity at 12 weeks of age in both male and female mice.
claims.source: When Dmp1Cre:Il6stf/f mice, which themselves had normal cortical porosity (Figure 5A) were crossed with Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, the resulting Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice exhibited normalised cortical porosity at 12 weeks of age in both male and female mice (Figure 5B,C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claims.claim: Levels of low- and mid-density bone were each significantly reduced in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice compared with the high levels observed in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice in both males and females.
claims.source: Normalisation was also observed in bone volume segregated by density. Levels of low- and mid-density bone were each significantly reduced in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice compared with the high levels observed in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice; this was observed in both males and females (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Female Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice showed a density pattern very similar to wild type mice of the same age.
claims.source: When the density profiles were assessed along the length of the bone, female Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice showed a pattern that was very similar to wild type mice of the same age (compare Figure 5E to Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data shown in Figures 5E and 3A.

claims.claim: The high volume of low-density bone seen in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice at the distal end was not observed in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice.
claims.source: The high volume of low-density bone seen in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice at the distal end (Figure 5E) was not observed in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claims.claim: The proportion of low density bone was significantly lower in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice compared to Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice in the distal region.
claims.source: When compared directly (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) the proportion of low density bone was significantly lower in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice compared to Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice in this region.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The level of mid-density bone was significantly lower in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice compared to Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
claims.source: The level of mid-density bone was also significantly lower in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice compared to Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), indicating a return to a phenotype similar to control mice (compare with Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The proportion of high density bone increased in both Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f and Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f female femora.
claims.source: The proportion of high density bone increased in both Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f and Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f female femora (Figure 5E,F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claims.claim: Deletion of gp130 from osteocytes normalises the delayed corticalisation of female Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
claims.source: These results indicate that deletion of gp130 from osteocytes normalises the delayed corticalisation of female Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data showing normalized cortical porosity and bone density distribution in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice.

claims.claim: Male Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice exhibited a lesser delay in corticalisation compared to females.
claims.source: Male Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice exhibited a lesser delay in corticalisation compared to females in our earlier study (Cho et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cho et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Male Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice exhibited the same differences compared to sex-matched Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice as seen in the females: a lower level of low density and mid-density bone, and no difference in high density bone.
claims.source: When gp130 was deleted from osteocytes, the male Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice exhibited the same differences compared to sex-matched Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice as seen in the females: a lower level of low density and mid-density bone, and no difference in high density bone (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–F.

claims.claim: Cortical consolidation specifically requires SOCS3 mediated suppression of IL-6 family cytokine signalling within osteocytes in both male and female mice.
claims.source: This indicates that cortical consolidation specifically requires SOCS3 mediated suppression of IL-6 family cytokine signalling within osteocytes in both male and female mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the rescue of the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f phenotype by gp130 deletion in both sexes.

claims.claim: There was no clear reduction in calcein labels in the metaphyseal cortex in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice compared to Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
claims.source: There was no clear reduction in calcein labels in the metaphyseal cortex in Dmp1Cre: Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice compared to Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice (Figure 6A,B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histological observations shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claims.claim: More cortical pores (containing blood vessels and sometimes bone marrow) were seen in the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice compared to Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice.
claims.source: Extensive double-labelled surfaces were observed in both genotypes in this region, but more cortical pores (containing blood vessels and sometimes bone marrow) were seen in the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histological observations shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claims.claim: The pore area was reduced in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f bone by approximately 60% compared to Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone.
claims.source: When quantified, the pore area was reduced in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f bone by approximately 60% (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histomorphometry data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Both osteoclasts and osteoblasts were detected within the pores in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone.
claims.source: Both osteoclasts and osteoblasts were detected within the pores in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone, and due to the reduction in pore area, the number of osteoclasts and osteoblasts were lower in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f bone than Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone (Figure 6D,E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histomorphometry data shown in Figures 6D and 6E.

claims.claim: Due to the reduction in pore area, the number of osteoclasts and osteoblasts were lower in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f bone than Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone.
claims.source: Both osteoclasts and osteoblasts were detected within the pores in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone, and due to the reduction in pore area, the number of osteoclasts and osteoblasts were lower in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f bone than Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone (Figure 6D,E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histomorphometry data shown in Figures 6D and 6E.

claims.claim: Voids in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f cortical bone exhibited large highly active osteoclasts within the newly forming cortex.
claims.source: When we assessed osteoclasts by TRAP staining, voids in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f cortical bone exhibited large highly active osteoclasts within the newly forming cortex (Figure 6F,G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TRAP staining shown in Figures 6F and 6G.

claims.claim: Resorption pits were observed in the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f metaphyses.
claims.source: Although murine osteoclasts do not usually demonstrate clear resorption pits, they were observed in this region in the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f metaphyses (Figure 6J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histological observations shown in Figure 6J.

claims.claim: The same region in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice rarely exhibited osteoclasts within the cortical pores.
claims.source: In contrast to the increased resorption observed in the tibial cortex in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f metaphyses, the same region in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice rarely exhibited osteoclasts within the cortical pores (Figure 6H,I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histological observations shown in Figures 6H and 6I.

claims.claim: The voids within the metaphyseal cortical bone of Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice had greater osteoclast numbers than in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice, yet there was no difference in osteoblast numbers between the genotypes.
claims.source: When quantified, the voids within the metaphyseal cortical bone of Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice had greater osteoclast numbers than in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice, yet there was no difference in osteoblast numbers between the genotypes (Figure 6K,L).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histomorphometry data shown in Figures 6K and 6L.

claims.claim: Acp5 (the gene for TRAP) was significantly less in flushed femoral samples from Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice compared to Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
claims.source: Analysis of flushed femoral samples, including mainly cortical bone provided some additional evidence of suppressed osteoclast formation in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice (Table 2); Acp5 (the gene for TRAP) was significantly less in these samples compared to Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by mRNA data shown in Table 2.

claims.claim: The reduction in Acp5 in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice was not associated with a significant change in RANKL mRNA (Tnfsf11).
claims.source: This was not associated with a significant change in RANKL mRNA (Tnfsf11), but OPG mRNA (Tnfrsf11b) levels were mildly, and barely statistically significantly, greater in samples from Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by mRNA data shown in Table 2.

claims.claim: OPG mRNA (Tnfrsf11b) levels were mildly, and barely statistically significantly, greater in samples from Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice compared to Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
claims.source: This was not associated with a significant change in RANKL mRNA (Tnfsf11), but OPG mRNA (Tnfrsf11b) levels were mildly, and barely statistically significantly, greater in samples from Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by mRNA data shown in Table 2.

claims.claim: There was a greater proportion of marrow-filled area within the calvarial bone (diploe) in 12 week old Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice compared to Dmp1Cre mice.
claims.source: To determine whether the cortical bone-specific effect on osteoclast formation could be detected at a second site, we carried out a preliminary analysis of calvarial bone from 12 week old Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f and Dmp1Cre mice collected in our original study (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B). There we observed a greater proportion of marrow-filled area within the calvarial bone (diploe) in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, and both a high level of calcein labelling, and abundant osteoclasts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Calvarial bone from 12 week old Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice showed both a high level of calcein labelling, and abundant osteoclasts.
claims.source: To determine whether the cortical bone-specific effect on osteoclast formation could be detected at a second site, we carried out a preliminary analysis of calvarial bone from 12 week old Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f and Dmp1Cre mice collected in our original study (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B). There we observed a greater proportion of marrow-filled area within the calvarial bone (diploe) in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, and both a high level of calcein labelling, and abundant osteoclasts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D.

claims.claim: The stimulatory effect of SOCS3 deletion on bone resorption occurs also in calvarial cortical bone that has not formed through trabecular consolidation.
claims.source: This confirms that the stimulatory effect of SOCS3 deletion on bone resorption occurs also in this cortical site that has not formed through trabecular consolidation.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the calvarial bone observations.

claims.claim: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice exhibited a more mature osteocyte canalicular network than Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
claims.source: The higher level of resorption in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f cortical bone was reflected in Ploton silver stains carried out at a slightly more distal location in the tibia. Indeed, in this more mature region, Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice exhibited a more mature osteocyte canalicular network than Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f (Figure 6M,N).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Ploton silver staining shown in Figures 6M and 6N.

claims.claim: The more mature osteocyte canalicular network in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice was indicated by a greater proportion of osteocyte cell bodies aligned parallel to the bone surface, and less cement lines within the cortex.
claims.source: This was indicated by a greater proportion of osteocyte cell bodies aligned parallel to the bone surface, and less cement lines within the cortex.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Ploton silver staining shown in Figures 6M and 6N.

claims.claim: The normalized structure in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice resembled the canalicular network of Dmp1Cre mice in the same region.
claims.source: The normalized structure resembled the canalicular network of Dmp1Cre mice in the same region (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with Ploton silver staining shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Normalization of cortical bone structure and maturation was associated with a significant reduction in phospho-STAT3 staining in osteocytes within the newly forming cortical bone.
claims.source: This normalization of cortical bone structure and maturation was associated with a significant reduction in phospho-STAT3 staining in osteocytes within the newly forming cortical bone (Figure 6O–Q).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 6O–Q.

claims.claim: For cortical consolidation to occur in the metaphysis, bone resorption must be suppressed, and this can be achieved by reducing gp130-dependent STAT3 phosphorylation in osteocytes.

claims.claim: The bone of Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice is more ductile.

claims.claim: Post-yield strain was significantly greater in both male and female Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice compared to the mutant Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.

claims.claim: The rescue of the strength defect in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice resulted from an improvement in the material quality of the cortical bone at the diaphysis, consistent with an improvement in cortical bone maturation.

claims.claim: Cortical bone formation includes both consolidation of structural elements and a transition from less organised and less mineralized bone to a mature lamellar structure.
claims.source: This study shows that cortical bone formation includes both consolidation of structural elements and a transition from less organised and less mineralized bone to a mature lamellar structure; new methods were developed to show this.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the data showing both morphological changes and density changes during cortical maturation.

claims.claim: Consolidation, maturation, and mechanical performance of the cortical structure requires suppression of STAT3 phosphorylation downstream of gp130 signalling in osteocytes.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the rescue of the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f phenotype by gp130 deletion.

claims.claim: When STAT3 phosphorylation is elevated, osteoclasts actively resorb the cortical structure, and formation of a lamellar structure is delayed.
claims.source: When STAT3 phosphorylation is elevated, osteoclasts actively resorb the cortical structure, and formation of a lamellar structure is delayed.

claims.claim: The transformation from a foamy woven bone cortex to a continuous cortical mass normally occurs between 10 and 14 days of age in C57BL/6 mice.

claims.claim: The transformation from a foamy woven bone cortex to a continuous cortical mass coincides with rapid longitudinal growth, and occurs prior to development of the femoral elliptical shape.
claims.source: This coincides with rapid longitudinal growth, and occurs prior to development of the femoral elliptical shape.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about bone development.

claims.claim: Cortical consolidation in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice occurred after both bone length and femoral shape are established.
claims.source: Since cortical consolidation in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice occurred after both bone length and femoral shape are established (Cho et al., 2017), we reasoned that their metaphyses could be used to track cortical consolidation without the complication of coincident changes in bone size and shape.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cho et al., 2017.

claims.claim: New bone deposited at the growth plate is progressively replaced with bone of higher mineral density as the bone ages.
claims.source: Closure of pores and increased mineralisation were both delayed in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, consistent with very early work showing that new bone deposited at the growth plate is progressively replaced with bone of higher mineral density as the bone ages (Enlow, 1962), and more recent work showing that adolescent bone has higher mineral content than infant bone (Zimmermann et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Enlow, 1962.

claims.claim: Adolescent bone has higher mineral content than infant bone.

claims.claim: Delayed cortical development in childhood could lead to compromised bone strength later in life.
claims.source: Clearly in the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, this process is slowed, a defect that may explain the reduced ductility of bone in the presence of normal bone mass in the 6 month old female Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice (Cho et al., 2017). claims.evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the implications of the findings in the mouse model for human health.

claims.source: Measurement of cortical porosity is a technique now common in micro-computed tomography studies of murine bone, but in this case, measuring the cortical pores in the metaphysis was challenging due to the difficulty of defining cortical and trabecular bone compartments.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about micro-CT methods.

claims.claim: At the resolution of a standard micro-CT instrument, the pores measured are significantly larger than osteocyte lacunae.
claims.source: At the resolution of a standard micro-CT instrument, the pores measured by this technique are significantly larger than osteocyte lacunae, and the majority of these pores are 'open pores' that connect with other pores, and with the top or bottom of the measurement region.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on technical knowledge about micro-CT resolution.

claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the measured pore size and comparison with histological observations.

claims.claim: It is often surmised that rodent bone does not remodel after the cortical shape has been established.
claims.source: We were surprised to observe a significant transformation from mid- to high-density bone in control mice between 12 and 15 weeks, after the cortical bone had formed. It is often surmised that rodent bone does not remodel after the cortical shape has been established.
claims.evidence: This claim represents a common assumption in the field.

claims.claim: Resorption cavities have only been described in murine bone after 52 weeks of age.
claims.source: However, although resorption cavities have only been described in murine bone after 52 weeks of age, lamellar bone content in bone increases even between 22 and 91 weeks of age; this occurs through an asymmetrical process where woven bone on the periosteum or the endocortical surface is resorbed and replaced by lamellar bone (Ferguson et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ferguson et al., 2003.

claims.claim: Lamellar bone content in bone increases even between 22 and 91 weeks of age in mice; this occurs through an asymmetrical process where woven bone on the periosteum or the endocortical surface is resorbed and replaced by lamellar bone.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ferguson et al., 2003.

claims.claim: The increase in mineral content in control mice between 12 and 15 weeks may reflect secondary mineralization of the established bone matrix.

claims.evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the mechanism of the observed density increase.

claims.claim: Multi-level Otsu thresholding provides a relatively simple way to measure the changes in bone maturation that occur with bone age in the same tissue samples.

claims.claim: The delayed metaphyseal development of Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone indicates that cortical formation requires SOCS3 expression by Dmp1Cre positive cells (most likely late-stage osteoblasts and osteocytes).
claims.source: The delayed metaphyseal development of Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f bone indicates that cortical formation requires SOCS3 expression by Dmp1Cre positive cells (most likely late-stage ostoblasts and osteocytes).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f phenotype.

claims.claim: The presence or absence of specific receptors in osteocytes is difficult to prove due to lack of purity of cell preparations, and the loss of the osteocyte phenotype when primary cells are cultured.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chia et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Osteoblast lineage cells do not express erythropoietin receptor.
claims.source: Although pharmacological treatment with erythropoietin modifies bone mass, and activates JAK/STAT signalling, we did not test the response to erythropoietin since in vivo lineage tracing studies have shown that osteoblast lineage cells do not express this receptor (Singbrant et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Singbrant et al., 2011.

claims.claim: G-CSFR mRNA (Csf3r) is not found in cultured osteoblast lineage cells (primary osteoblasts, osteoblast cell lines, and the MLO-Y4 osteocyte-like cell line).
claims.source: G-CSF did not induce a STAT3 phosphorylation response even in control animals, consistent with earlier studies reporting that G-CSFR mRNA (Csf3r) is not found in cultured osteoblast lineage cells (primary osteoblasts, osteoblast cell lines, and the MLO-Y4 osteocyte-like cell line) (Katayama et al., 2006).

claims.claim: IL-11 stimulates STAT3 phosphorylation in primary calvarial osteoblasts.

Ho, unpublished data).

claims.evidence: This claim is based on unpublished data mentioned in the manuscript.

claims.claim: At least three members of the IL-6 family (OSM, LIF, IL-11) may require suppression to enable cortical maturation.

claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the STAT3 phosphorylation data.

claims.claim: gp130 is a signalling receptor for a wide range of bone-active cytokines.
claims.source: While we identified that gp130 is the receptor that must be suppressed for cortical consolidation, we did not identify a responsible hyperactive gp130-dependent cytokine. claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sims, 2015 and Sims, 2016.

claims.claim: IL-11, OSM and LIF are all required for normal osteoclast formation.
claims.source: Our western blot data suggest that IL-11, OSM and LIF are all candidates. All three showed extended STAT3 phosphorylation in the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, and all three are required for normal osteoclast formation (Sims et al., 2005; Walker et al., 2010; Poulton et al., 2012).

results.result: Cortical bone maturation involves reduction in cortical porosity and transition from low to high density bone, continuing after cortical shape is established. This process is delayed in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 and C46-C55 provide converging evidence from micro-CT imaging showing that control mice undergo cortical porosity reduction and density increases between 12-16 weeks, even after femoral length plateaus (C47). The Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice show delayed but ongoing cortical consolidation (C48, C51). Pseudocolorized micro-CT videos and quantitative data support both morphological and density changes.

results.result: Multi-level Otsu thresholding reveals that cortical maturation involves replacement of low-density bone with high-density bone. Control mice show 14-fold increase in high-density bone between 12-15 weeks, while Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice have elevated low-density bone.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C66 describe a novel quantitative method showing significant changes in bone density distribution. The data demonstrate that control mice transition from predominantly low/mid-density to high-density bone (C60-C62), while Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice maintain higher proportions of low-density bone (C63-C65). Statistical significance is reported with appropriate methods.

results.result: Slice-by-slice analysis along the metaphysis reveals a spatial gradient of bone maturation, with more mature bone at greater distances from the growth plate. This allows assessment of cortical maturation at a single time point.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C74 describe a methodological advance showing that bone density increases with distance from the growth plate (C68, C71). The data demonstrate that a single time point can capture the maturation process (C73), and that bone continues to mature after cortical consolidation (C74). The reasoning is sound and supported by quantitative micro-CT data.

results.result: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice show delayed cortical maturation with elevated low-density bone throughout the metaphysis at both 12 and 15 weeks, though they eventually accumulate high-density bone similar to controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C86 provide detailed characterization of the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f phenotype using the slice-by-slice analysis. The data show doubled low-density bone in proximal regions (C76), delayed high-density bone accumulation (C78, C80-C81), and persistence of immature bone characteristics (C82-C84). Multiple complementary measurements support the conclusion of delayed maturation (C85-C86).

results.result: Histological analysis confirms that Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice have immature cortical bone at 16 weeks, characterized by rounded osteocytes, lack of ordered orientation, and abundant cement lines reflecting rapid remodeling rather than lamellar bone formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C91 provide histological validation of the micro-CT findings. Ploton silver staining shows mature lamellar bone in controls (C87) versus woven bone with disorganized osteocytes in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice (C88). The interpretation that cement lines reflect remodeling rather than cartilage retention is supported by prior work (C89-C90).

results.result: At 26 weeks, female Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice have normal bone mass but significantly altered bone density distribution with less high- and mid-density bone and more low-density bone than controls.
results.evaluation: Claim C92 demonstrates that the maturation defect persists to 26 weeks despite normal total bone mass. This is supported by the three-tiered density analysis showing significant differences in bone quality. This finding has important implications for understanding long-term consequences of delayed cortical maturation.

results.result: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice show prolonged STAT3 phosphorylation specifically in response to gp130-signaling cytokines (IL-11, LIF, OSM) but not leptin or G-CSF, with elevated basal phospho-STAT3 in osteocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C99 identify the specific signaling pathway affected by SOCS3 deletion. Western blot data show prolonged STAT3 phosphorylation for IL-6 family cytokines (C93) but not leptin/G-CSF (C94). Immunohistochemistry confirms elevated phospho-STAT3 in osteocytes in vivo (C98). The lack of basal differences by western blot (C96) is appropriately explained by technical limitations (C97).

results.result: A new Il6st-flox mouse (Dmp1Cre:Il6stf/f) was generated to avoid potential confounding effects of soluble gp130. This mouse shows reduced Il6st transcription and phenocopies the previous gp130 deletion model with low trabecular bone mass and normal cortical porosity.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C105 describe important methodological validation. The new mouse model targets exon 1 to eliminate all gp130 isoforms (C102) and shows the expected phenotype (C103-C104), confirming that previous findings were due to loss of gp130 signaling rather than soluble gp130 production. The normal cortical porosity in Dmp1Cre:Il6stf/f mice (C105) is crucial for the rescue experiments.

results.result: Deletion of gp130 in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice (creating Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice) rescues the cortical maturation defect, normalizing cortical porosity and bone density distribution in both male and female mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C116 provide strong genetic evidence that gp130 signaling mediates the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f phenotype. The double mutant shows normalized cortical porosity (C106), reduced low- and mid-density bone (C107), and density patterns similar to wild-type (C108-C111). The rescue occurs in both sexes (C115-C116), demonstrating that SOCS3-mediated suppression of gp130 signaling is required for cortical consolidation.

results.result: The rescue of cortical maturation in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice is associated with reduced cortical pore area, decreased osteoclast numbers within cortical voids, and reduced osteoclast marker expression, while osteoblast numbers remain unchanged.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C128 identify the cellular mechanism of rescue. Histomorphometry shows ~60% reduction in pore area (C119), decreased osteoclast numbers (C121, C125), and reduced Acp5 expression (C126), while osteoblast numbers are unchanged (C125). The presence of resorption pits in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice (C123) and their absence in the rescue (C124) provides visual confirmation. The mild OPG increase (C128) may contribute but is not the primary mechanism.

results.result: The stimulatory effect of SOCS3 deletion on bone resorption also occurs in calvarial cortical bone, which forms through intramembranous rather than endochondral ossification.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C131 extend the findings to a second anatomical site. Preliminary analysis shows increased diploe area (C129) with high calcein labeling and abundant osteoclasts (C130) in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f calvariae. This demonstrates that the mechanism is not specific to endochondral bone formation (C131), strengthening the generalizability of the findings.

results.result: Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice show more mature osteocyte canalicular networks with aligned osteocytes, fewer cement lines, and reduced phospho-STAT3 staining in cortical bone compared to Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C136 provide histological evidence that the rescue includes improved bone maturation at the cellular level. Ploton silver staining shows better osteocyte organization (C132-C133) resembling control mice (C134). The correlation with reduced phospho-STAT3 (C135) supports the mechanistic link between gp130-STAT3 signaling and cortical consolidation (C136).

results.result: Deletion of gp130 in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice restores bone mechanical properties, approximately doubling post-yield deformation and post-yield strain in both sexes, indicating improved bone ductility and material quality.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C142 demonstrate functional rescue of bone strength. Three-point bending tests show doubled post-yield deformation (C138) and increased post-yield strain (C141) in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f:Il6stf/f mice. The interpretation that this reflects improved material quality and ductility (C140, C142) is reasonable given the normalization of cortical structure. The reduced yield force in males (C139) is appropriately interpreted as increased ductility rather than weakness.

results.result: Cortical bone formation includes both structural consolidation and transition to mature lamellar bone, requiring suppression of gp130-STAT3 signaling in osteocytes. Elevated STAT3 phosphorylation leads to increased osteoclastic resorption and delayed lamellar bone formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C145 synthesize the major findings into a coherent model. The data support that cortical maturation involves both morphological and compositional changes (C143), that gp130-STAT3 suppression is required (C144), and that elevated STAT3 drives osteoclast activity and delays maturation (C145). This is well-supported by the genetic, cellular, and mechanical data presented.

results.result: Multi-level Otsu thresholding provides a simple, non-invasive, non-destructive method to measure bone maturation that could be applied to various disease models and potentially to human CT scans or archived specimens.
results.evaluation: Claims C163-C167 describe the methodological contribution. The Otsu-based method successfully quantified maturation in a model where traditional cortical/trabecular segmentation failed (C163-C164). The suggestions for broader applications (C165-C167) are reasonable given the method's characteristics, though these remain to be validated. The method represents a significant technical advance for the field.

results.result: The delayed cortical maturation in Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice indicates that SOCS3 in osteocytes is required for cortical formation. Testing of candidate cytokines revealed that IL-11, LIF, and OSM all induce prolonged STAT3 phosphorylation in SOCS3-deficient bone.
results.evaluation: Claims C168-C175 describe the systematic identification of relevant cytokines. The approach of testing STAT3 responses to avoid cell culture artifacts is well-justified (C169). The exclusion of erythropoietin (C170) and G-CSF (C171) based on prior literature is appropriate. The positive responses to OSM, LIF, and IL-11 (C172-C174) identify at least three cytokines requiring suppression (C175).

results.result: While gp130 is the receptor requiring suppression, the specific hyperactive cytokine(s) remain unidentified. IL-11, OSM, and LIF are candidates as they showed prolonged STAT3 phosphorylation and are required for osteoclast formation. These cytokines likely must be suppressed to limit RANKL production by osteocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C176-C181 appropriately acknowledge limitations while proposing a mechanism. The identification of multiple candidate cytokines (C177) is supported by the STAT3 phosphorylation data and literature on osteoclast formation. The speculation about cardiotrophin-1 (C178) and dismissal of CNTFR-binding cytokines (C179-C180) are reasonable. The proposed mechanism involving RANKL (C181) is logical but requires further validation.

results.result: The effects of gp130-dependent cytokines on cortical consolidation appear to be local and site-specific, as high osteoclast formation was not observed in trabecular bone of Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, indicating separate mechanisms control osteoclast formation in trabecular versus cortical bone.
results.evaluation: Claims C182-C185 identify an important spatial specificity in the phenotype. The observation that trabecular bone is unaffected (C182) indicates distinct regulatory mechanisms (C183). The citations to prior work showing differential effects (C184) support this interpretation, though the mechanisms remain unclear (C185). This observation is important for understanding bone biology but requires further investigation.

results.result: Potential mechanisms for differential cytokine effects in cortical versus trabecular bone include differences in mechanical strain (with IL-11, OSM, SOCS3, and STAT3 being mechanically responsive) or differences in vascularization and osteoclast precursor supply.
results.evaluation: Claims C186-C190 propose speculative mechanisms for the observed spatial differences. While the cited literature supports that these cytokines are mechanically responsive (C187) and that STAT3 is required for mechanical responses (C188), and that LIF regulates vascular formation at the growth plate (C190), these remain hypotheses requiring experimental validation. The speculation is reasonable but not directly tested.

results.result: Preliminary analysis suggests that the mechanisms controlling cortical consolidation also exist in calvarial bone formed through intramembranous ossification.
results.evaluation: Claim C191 is supported by the preliminary calvarial data (C129-C131) showing similar phenotypes in both endochondral and intramembranous bone. However, the analysis is described as preliminary, suggesting limited sample size or depth of analysis. The conclusion is reasonable but would benefit from more extensive validation.

results.result: A new Il6st-flox mouse was developed to eliminate potential confounding effects of soluble gp130 from the previous model. The phenocopy confirms that the earlier phenotype resulted from loss of gp130 signaling rather than soluble gp130 production, and that gp130 signaling in osteocytes maintains trabecular bone formation and limits cortical width.
results.evaluation: Claims C192-C207 provide detailed justification for the new mouse model. The extensive background on soluble gp130 isoforms (C194-C201) and their inhibitory activities supports the rationale for the new model. The phenocopy (C205) definitively resolves the question of whether the previous phenotype was due to loss of signaling or gain of soluble inhibitor (C206). This represents rigorous validation of prior findings.

results.result: The initial stages of cortical development appear similar in mice and humans, both passing through a transitional 'coarse compact' woven bone phase before remodeling. The key difference between small and large mammals occurs after this phase, with the mouse model relevant to early human cortical development.
results.evaluation: Claims C208-C218 address the translational relevance of the mouse model. The comparison to human bone development (C209-C210) and the identification of the transitional phase (C211-C215) are well-supported by citations. The inference that initial steps are similar across species (C217) is reasonable based on the shared transitional phase. The acknowledgment that applicability to later stages remains uncertain (C218) is appropriately cautious.

results.result: Background on cortical bone development: trabeculae from the growth plate coalesce to form cortical shell, woven bone is replaced by lamellar bone, and the cellular/molecular mechanisms controlling this process remain undefined. Studying this process is challenging due to rapid growth and difficulty identifying fixed positions during bone lengthening.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C27 provide well-cited background establishing the knowledge gap. The descriptions of normal bone development (C14-C21) are supported by appropriate citations. The identification of methodological challenges (C23-C27) justifies the experimental approach. This represents accurate representation of prior knowledge and study rationale.

results.result: Background on clinical significance: peak bone mass predicts fracture risk, trabecular abnormalities affect cortical structure, trabecularization in older individuals leads to fragility, cortical bone determines long bone strength, and current osteoporosis treatments are less effective at cortical sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C35 establish the clinical importance of understanding cortical bone development. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to clinical literature. This background effectively motivates the study by connecting basic bone biology to clinical outcomes and treatment limitations.

results.result: Background on SOCS3 and cortical development: prior work showed that SOCS3 deletion in osteocytes delays cortical consolidation, SOCS3 inhibits multiple cytokine receptors (leptin, G-CSF, gp130), these cytokines can affect bone, but IL-6 deletion does not rescue the phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C45 provide essential background from prior work. The citations to previous studies (C36-C37, C44-C45) establish the foundation for the current investigation. The description of SOCS3 function (C39-C40) and potential candidate cytokines (C41-C43) sets up the rationale for identifying which receptor must be suppressed. This represents accurate representation of prior findings.

results.result: The transformation from foamy woven bone to continuous cortical mass normally occurs at 10-14 days in mice, coinciding with rapid growth. In Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice, this occurs after bone length and shape are established, allowing study without confounding size changes. Delayed cortical development may compromise later bone strength.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C151 explain the rationale for using the Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f model. The timing of normal cortical consolidation (C146-C147) and the delayed timing in the mutant (C148) are supported by citations. The speculation about long-term consequences (C151) is reasonable given the 26-week data (C92) but remains somewhat speculative regarding human health implications.

results.result: Technical details of cortical porosity measurement: standard micro-CT measures pores significantly larger than osteocyte lacunae. Control mice have few pores (5-10,000 μm³), while Dmp1Cre:Socs3f/f mice have much larger pores (146,000 μm³) with complex geometry, large enough to contain blood vessels, osteoclasts, osteoblasts, and marrow.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C158 provide important technical context for interpreting the porosity measurements. The size comparisons to osteocyte lacunae (C154, C156) and the characterization of pore complexity (C157) help readers understand what is being measured. The inference that pores can contain various cell types (C158) is reasonable based on the size measurements and histological observations.

results.result: Discussion of bone remodeling in mice: contrary to common assumptions, rodent bone continues to mature after cortical shape is established. Lamellar bone content increases between 22-91 weeks through asymmetrical remodeling. The rapid density increase in control mice between 12-15 weeks may reflect secondary mineralization.
results.evaluation: Claims C159-C162 challenge common assumptions about rodent bone remodeling. The citation to Ferguson et al. (C160-C161) supports that remodeling continues in older mice. The speculation about secondary mineralization (C162) is reasonable given the rapid time course but remains speculative. This discussion appropriately contextualizes the findings within existing knowledge.
